opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting thing is that the cost of running an experiment has collapsed. In research, the bottleneck has rarely been ideas. Everyone has a notebook full of "wouldn't it be interesting if..." The bottleneck is that each idea takes a few days of plumbing: writing the data loader, wiring up the training loop, debugging some shape mismatch at 2 a.m., making the plots. So you ration your curiosity. You only test the ideas you're already fairly confident in.

With coding assistants, I can describe an experiment in a paragraph and have a working version in twenty minutes. That changes your psychology as a researcher. You start testing the weird ideas, the ones with a 5% prior, because they're cheap now. A lot of important discoveries come from that tail.

What I find most promising, though, is less "the model writes code for me" and more that it's starting to close the loop. It can run the experiment, look at the loss curve, notice something's off, form a hypothesis about why, and try a fix. It's not great at deciding *which* questions matter. That taste is still very human. But the inner loop of hypothesis, implement, measure, revise is becoming something you can delegate. When that happens, one researcher starts to look like a small lab.

The caveat is verification. These systems will confidently report a result that comes from a bug, like data leaking into the eval set or a seed that happened to work. So the skill that becomes more valuable is knowing how to check whether a result is real. Good scientists have always been paranoid about their own results, and now you have to be paranoid at a much higher throughput.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I find most promising isn't that these systems are generating brilliant new ideas. They mostly aren't, yet. What's promising is that they've collapsed the cost of the boring parts of science, and the boring parts were always the bottleneck.

If you look at how research actually happens, maybe five percent of a researcher's time is the creative insight, and the other ninety-five percent is plumbing. You have a hypothesis, and then you spend two weeks writing the data loader, fixing the evaluation harness, getting the baseline to reproduce, realizing you had an off-by-one in the normalization. That's where ideas go to die. Most hypotheses never get tested, not because they're bad, but because testing them is too expensive relative to the expected payoff.

Coding assistants change that calculus. I can have a half-formed idea at eleven at night, describe it in a paragraph, and have a working experiment running before I go to sleep. The quality of the idea hasn't changed, but the number of ideas I actually try has gone up by maybe an order of magnitude. And science is fundamentally a search process. If you make sampling ten times cheaper, you find more things, even if each sample is no smarter than before.

The second thing I'd point to is reproducibility. For years we've had this embarrassing situation where a paper comes out, the code is a mess or missing, and nobody can tell whether the result is real. Now you can hand a model the paper and say, reimplement this, and within an hour you have an independent implementation and a clear signal about whether the claim holds up. That's going to raise the floor on what gets published, or at least on what gets believed.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that these systems are good at being a tireless, slightly dumb research partner. They'll run the ablation you were too lazy to run. They'll check the thing you assumed was fine. In robotics, where I spend most of my time, so much of the work is just exhaustively checking that your pipeline isn't lying to you, and having something that does that without getting bored is a real multiplier.

So I'd say the promise today is less about AI as a scientist and more about AI as a lab that never sleeps. The genuinely new ideas are still coming from people. But the distance between having an idea and knowing whether it's true has shrunk dramatically, and historically that distance is what has determined how fast a field moves.

astra-6.text:
I think the most promising thing is how much they shorten the loop between having an idea and running an experiment. A lot of research involves work that isn’t itself the central insight: implementing a baseline, getting two libraries to work together, writing the evaluation, figuring out why something crashed. Coding assistants can take a lot of that off your plate.

That changes which ideas you’re willing to try. If testing a hunch takes a week, you have to be pretty selective. If you can get an initial result in an afternoon, you can explore things that sound a little silly but might teach you something.

The part where I still want a human deeply involved is interpreting the result. Did we actually test the hypothesis? Is there a bug or some leakage? Does this result distinguish between two explanations? Generating code is useful, but the scientific value comes from closing that loop with an experiment you can trust.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find most promising is that coding assistants make it much cheaper to try an idea. A lot of research involves this gap between “I wonder if this works” and actually getting an experiment running. You have to implement a baseline, figure out somebody else’s code, debug the data pipeline, and make the plots. If an assistant can take care of more of that, you can spend more time deciding what experiment is worth doing and interpreting the result.

The interesting next step is closing that loop: the system runs an experiment, looks at the result, and decides what to try next. You can already imagine that being useful in settings where experiments are cheap and feedback is clear. The harder question is whether it can tell when a result is scientifically meaningful. Getting a number to go up is one thing; figuring out whether you’ve learned something is another.
